analysis.title: Weekly Economic Commentary (October 30, 2026): The Economics Of The U.S. Midterm Elections, Downsides Of Diminished Immigration, Gulf Under Pressure
key_insights: Northern Trust expects the 2026 U.S. midterms to have little impact on the U.S. economy and says it may not alter its forecasts. The largest fiscal blocks, last year's One Big Beautiful Bill reconciliation package and the immigration-enforcement funding bill passed earlier this year, are already in place.

Most analysts expect the House to flip to Democratic control, while the Senate is a closer call. Even with a Democratic win, the majority is likely too narrow to pass significant legislation. A filibuster needs 60 votes to overcome and a presidential veto needs 67 votes to override.
If Republicans hold both chambers, Northern Trust still does not expect major legislation. Further spending or tax cuts would widen the deficit and risk renewed bond market tensions.

Senate control matters most for Cabinet, court and Federal Reserve appointments. A Democratic Senate could block highly partisan nominees, but agency leadership can be maintained through acting appointments under the Vacancy Act.

The debt ceiling will be an early task for the next Congress. It was set at $41.1 trillion by last year's reconciliation bill and stood at $40.2 trillion at end of September. The Bipartisan Policy Center estimates the U.S. runs out of borrowing room in the first half of next year.
Northern Trust says a technical default threat would add to worries about Treasury debt at a time when yields are already rising. It links the deficit to the bond sell-off.

Federal spending is on a continuing resolution likely to be extended until after the new Congress is seated in January. The annual defense appropriations act was not passed in 2026. Substantial fiscal reform is expected to be deferred.

The fiscal 2026 national deficit was just shy of $2 trillion, elevated by tariff refunds. Northern Trust says fixed income markets would welcome a reduction and notes that deficit reduction in the 1990s came under divided government.

On other policy areas, the report sees few federal sponsors for AI regulation, with data center rules left to states and municipalities. Trade policy will stay White House led, heavy immigration enforcement is likely to continue, and unilateral Middle East military actions are legally questioned but unlikely to be halted.
Northern Trust says unwinding the Middle East conflict would ease pressure on energy prices and improve the inflation and affordability outlook.

U.S. immigration has retreated substantially since early 2025 after Congressional Budget Office estimates of annual traffic above 3 million in 2023 and 2024, about three times the normal level. Legal and illegal immigration combined are now at very low levels.

Reduced immigration is limiting labor supply. Job creation is well below typical expansion levels while joblessness stays very low, and the Federal Reserve Board estimated earlier this year that the monthly payroll growth needed to hold unemployment constant has fallen significantly.

Labor stress is concentrated in agriculture, construction, hospitality, care giving and food processing, and border states are hit harder. Northern Trust sees little evidence so far that foreign-born worker shortages are raising wages or inflation, and attributes the current construction worker shortage more to the AI buildout.
Slower population growth also slows aggregate demand growth, which takes pressure off the price level. Northern Trust expects the impact of reduced immigration to be felt more keenly over time.

The IMF now expects GCC economies to contract 4.8% this year, versus a 2% expansion projected in April. Kuwait and Qatar face particularly steep declines and Oman is the only regional economy expected to grow.

Oil and gas production fell by as much as 86% in the most exposed Gulf nations because of production disruptions and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Higher energy prices only partly offset the lower volumes.

GCC non-oil GDP is expected to shrink 0.8% in 2026, as tourism, aviation, logistics, construction and financial services have been hit by falling tourist arrivals, air-traffic restrictions, higher transport costs and weaker confidence.

Restoring oil exports is quicker than restoring tourism, trade networks or postponed investment, so recovering energy shipments have not yet produced a broader Gulf recovery. The IMF expects GCC growth of 9.1% in 2027, but output would stay below the pre-war trajectory for several years.

macro_indicators.interpretation: The Bipartisan Policy Center estimates borrowing room runs out in the first half of next year, making the debt ceiling an early item for the new Congress and a possible source of Treasury market stress.

macro_indicators.reading: just shy of $2 trillion in fiscal 2026
macro_indicators.interpretation: The deficit was elevated by tariff refunds. Northern Trust links it to the bond sell-off and says fixed income markets would welcome a reduction.
A reversal from the 2% expansion the IMF projected in April, driven by the Middle East war and the Strait of Hormuz closure.
Shows the conflict is hitting tourism, aviation, logistics, construction and financial services as well as energy.
A sharp rebound is expected as energy production and trade normalize, though output would remain below the pre-war trajectory for several years.

macro_indicators.reading: down as much as 86% in the most exposed nations
macro_indicators.interpretation: Production disruptions and the Strait of Hormuz closure curtailed hydrocarbon output, and higher prices only partly offset the lower volumes.

risk_factors: Renewed bond market tensions if Republicans hold both chambers and pass further spending or tax cuts that widen the deficit.
A debt ceiling standoff in the first half of next year could raise worries about Treasury debt while yields are already rising.
Labor shortages from reduced immigration in agriculture, construction, hospitality, care giving and food processing, with the effect expected to grow over time.
Prolonged Gulf economic weakness because confidence, tourism, trade networks and postponed investment recover more slowly than oil exports.
Continued Middle East conflict keeps pressure on energy prices, inflation and affordability.
charts_described: Chart titled U.S. Unauthorized Immigration plots entries, exits and net from 2014 to 2024, with the caption that net entry to the United States has fallen substantially.

Chart of U.S. occupations with high fractions of foreign-born workers shows 42%, 39%, 35% and 26% for farming, fishing and forestry, building and grounds maintenance, construction and extraction, and food preparation and serving.
geopolitical: War in the Middle East has pressured inflation and interest rates, and the Strait of Hormuz was closed, severely curtailing Gulf hydrocarbon activity.
Unilateral U.S. actions in the Middle East have been legally questioned, but the report says they are not likely to be halted by Congress.
The Gulf conflict has cut tourist arrivals and air traffic in GCC economies, and confidence may take a long time to restore even after the fighting stops.
Heavy U.S. tariffs remain in place and trade policy is expected to stay White House led, with Congress having delegated its powers to the executive branch.

tension_points.bull_case: Northern Trust says the divided-government outcome could produce common ground to reduce or contain outlays, as in the 1990s, which fixed income markets would welcome.
tension_points.bear_case: Neither party has made fiscal discipline a key message, so substantial fiscal reform is likely deferred. A debt ceiling showdown could add to Treasury debt worries while yields are rising.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Republicans holding both chambers and passing further spending or tax cuts would deepen the deficit and risk renewed bond market tensions.
